Bose’s second-generation QuietComfort Headphones in Dewdrop Mint, Eucalyptus Green, and Hazelnut Taupe are down to $199 from $359 ahead of Black Friday, saving you $160 and bringing them to their lowest price yet, according to price trackers. Weighing around 8.1 ounces, they’re among the lightest premium noise-canceling headphones, with generously padded earcups and a cushioned headband that spreads pressure without gripping too tightly, making them comfortable to wear for extended periods. They’re also easy to pack for travel, as the earcups fold and swivel for storage in the included hard-shell carrying case. The removable earpads are another welcome touch, since you can replace them as they wear down without having to retire the entire pair.

Comfort aside, noise cancellation is another area where these headphones deliver, doing a particularly good job of reducing lower-frequency rumble and background chatter, though some higher-pitched voices can still come through, notes this PCMag review. As for their sound profile, it leans warm and bass-forward, with deep lows that suit bass-heavy genres, while the companion app adds Bose Immersive Audio for spatial sound and lets you create customized listening profiles—the three-band EQ is fairly basic, though, so anyone who likes fine-tuning their sound may find the adjustment options limiting.

Connectivity, too, brings some useful upgrades over the previous generation, including Bluetooth 5.4, multipoint pairing for two devices, Google Fast Pair, and lossless audio over USB-C. That same USB-C port lets you charge the headphones while you listen, and the included USB-C-to-3.5mm cable covers standard headphone jacks, including the ones on in-flight entertainment systems. That said, battery life is less impressive, topping out at 24 hours with ANC enabled, although a 15-minute charge adds around 2.5 hours of playback. Wireless audio is also limited to the standard AAC and SBC codecs, with no support for the higher-quality aptX Adaptive—a feature available on Bose’s QuietComfort Ultra Headphones.

#3379. Nintendo Switch games running natively on Apple TV using Claude Code port

A Redditor has just released an open-source project allowing Switch and Switch 2 games to run natively on Apple TV.

So far, both Super Mario Odyssey and Animal Crossing: New Horizons are running, with work ongoing on The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom …

We’ve seen people using Claude Code to do some pretty wild things, like reverse engineering Adobe’s pro apps in order to create open-source versions of them. The latest example is a Redditor who’s created an open-source project called TVport to recompile Nintendo games from the Switch and Switch 2 to Apple TV.

Redditor FloatingFalafel shared the work on GitHub. They’ve so far ported three games to Apple TV, with one of them still a work in progress.

I have been working on a fork of nxnative that recompiles your OG Switch and Switch 2 dumps for AppleTV. Currently, this only works on a game-by-game basis. Most games run essentially the same on the switch, but some load textures into memory differently and need to be diagnosed and fixed before the game will run properly. My hope is to find outliers during this beta so more fixes can be added into the program, making it a seamless experience […]

Super Mario Odyssey – Runs at 60FPS, very slight stutters on occasion, and some audio issues around waterfalls specifically.

Animal Crossing: Horizon – Runs at 30FPS, zero issues so far on my plays.

Zelda: TOTK – Still being worked on, runs at 30FPS, gets thermal throttled. I have a work around for the thermal throttle. I have a render scale selection set at 75% and I am working on adding MetalFX upscaling.

They note you’ll need the 4th-gen Apple TV with its 8GB RAM in order to support some games, though these ones run on the 3rd-gen box.

Another Redditor is working on porting Nintendo 64 games to Apple TV using an app called Nativecade. How long any of these types of projects will survive is anyone’s guess.

#3377. Meet the Vigodas: Conan O’Brien Plays Out His Teenage Dream With L.A. Cover Band

When Conan O’Brien takes the stage at the Teragram Ballroom in downtown Los Angeles on Friday night, he’s wearing tight black jeans, a custom black jacket sporting the band’s name, and a wide smile. He greets the crowd by asking how many people had seen his cover band, the Vigodas. A few shout that they had, but the vast majority were there to see him for the first time. And despite his fame, that makes sense. Though he’s probably one of the most recognizable and beloved people in Hollywood, at this point, the band has only done about 10 shows around Southern California since premiering in August.

They draw a wide range of fans. Some know him from his days hosting Late Night, while others seem to be dedicated listeners to his long-running interview podcast, Conan O’Brien Needs a Friend —a smattering appear young enough to have only seen clips of him during his network heyday. The band run through more than a dozen covers — from Elvis Presley and Elvis Costello to Bo Diddley and John Lennon — an eclectic mix of rock & roll spanning the 1950s through the 1980s that is probably best described as the music that won’t get out of O’Brien’s head.

“When I was in college, when everyone else was starting to listen to U2 and Oingo Boingo, I was into hardcore rockabilly,” O’Brien, 63, tells Rolling Stone backstage before the show, running his fingers through the front of his ginger mane, which leaves it in a four-inch wave above his head. “I had the hair for it.” He loved the raucous sounds of Jerry Lee Lewis and early Elvis Presley. “Over the years, I would pick up these songs that were like adrenaline,” he says. “One of them is Ronnie Hawkins’ version of ‘40 Days,’” which they play later during their set.

Though the crowd never seems to break a sweat, they’re engaged through the hour-plus set, occasionally singing along and doing little solo swing dances in place. (There are also a surprising number of couples making out.) But the best part of the night is the overwhelming joy on O’Brien’s face as he jams onstage with four other guys 20 years his junior, whom he only met a few months ago but became fast friends.  Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

O’Brien is probably still best known for his decades as a talk-show host, but it was the podcast that launched the band, he says, when he had singer Norah Jones on in May 2023. “I’ve known Norah over the years, and she always remembered me having a guitar whenever she would come do the late-night show,” O’Brien says. “She said, ‘How’s the guitar going?’ And I said, ‘You know, it’s kind of sad because I don’t really have anyone to play with, and I need someone to kind of kick my ass and help my game.’ She said, ‘I know a guy.’”

The guy was guitarist Jason Roberts, who’d played in Jones’ band for half a decade. He started giving O’Brien lessons, and they would nerd out about their shared love of the Beatles. “We text about the Beatles a lot,” Roberts says later. “We just both love the Beatles so much.”

About six months ago, O’Brien asked Roberts if he’d be down to take their lessons to the next level. “He was just like, ‘Can you help me put a band together?’” Roberts remembers. “And I said, “I know the exact guys for this.” O’Brien tells the same story. “A week later, we’re in Hollywood, and we’re playing,” he says. “I’m just floating, so happy.”

They named themselves after the late actor Abe Vigoda — another towering figure with an expressive face, best known for his roles in The Godfather and Barney Miller. “Abe was a fixture on my old late show, he did hundreds of bits for us, and he was a sweet and hilarious man. I always knew his iconic mug was the face of our band,” says O’Brien. He had never played in a band as a teenager, but always wanted to. “For years and years and years, you could argue that the only reason I wanted a late-night show was so I could have a band,” he says. Back when he was working with the Max Weinberg 7, and later Jimmy Vivino and the Basic Cable Band, he would join them to jam every time they had rehearsal. “I’d put on a guitar and I would play with them and sing songs,” he says. “We had a good repertoire. And then when I went through my Tonight Show madness” — referring to the six months he spent behind the desk of the NBC institution from 2009 to 2010 — “we went out on the road and we did a comedy show, but also it had a lot of music in it too, and that was my happy place.”  Related Content Jack White, Barack Obama, Conan O’Brien Celebrate Stephen Colbert as ‘The Late Show’ Ends Conan O’Brien to Bring His Irreverent Comedy to the Oscars for Third Consecutive Year Jimmy Kimmel Forms Cover Band With Conan O’Brien, Jon Stewart at Netflix Is a Joke Fest Oscars Boss Reveals What You Didn’t See on TV: ‘Sinners’ Performance Ran Long, Speech Snafus, More

O’Brien seems comfortable as a cover man, satisfied to reinterpret the music he loves — often by speeding them up. A few years ago, he ran into Beverly D’Angelo at a party, and she commented to him at just how fast his version of “40 Days” was when she heard it on tour. Earlier this year, when the Rolling Stones asked him to introduce them and their new album at a concert in Brooklyn, he ran into Keith Richards backstage. “Keith said to me, he said, ‘I heard your ‘Monkey Business,’” O’Brien says, referring to the Chuck Berry cover he recorded with Jack White for 2010’s Live at Third Man. O’Brien was surprised he knew who he was, much less had heard his 16-year-old record. “You’re kidding,” he replied. “[Keith] went, ‘You sound like a fucking auctioneer.’” O’Brien laughs. “He’s not wrong.”

Part of the joy of the band is the excuse to tour different venues in Los Angeles. Their first show was at Permanent Records Roadhouse, a tiny club in East L.A. where they played as a surprise guest after Fred Armison’s regularly scheduled set. Since then, they’ve had a tour of Los Angeles’ finest small stages, from the Troubadour to the Lodge Room to the Moroccan Lounge. “I’m a connoisseur of kooky backstages,” he says, remembering a time he hung out with his friend and idol Bob Newhart backstage at the Chicago Theatre. “I had a goofy dressing room, and Bob Newhart said, ‘Conan, no matter what you achieve in show business, whenever you get to the theater and they show you your dressing room, there’s always a piece of dead brown lettuce on the floor. That’s just the way it is.” He smiles at the thought. “It’s very humbling.” Trending Stories Good Riddance to the Cybertruck, the Chariot of the Dumbest Gods 'SNL' Cold Open: James Talarico Crashes Trump's Midterm Postmortem A Jesuit Priest Explains How He Facilitated Bob Dylan’s Meeting With the Pope 'SNL' Weekend Update Drags Trump Over Midterm Drubbing, Stephen Miller Promotion

Aside from getting to see the bowels of these Art Deco monuments, the other point of the band, O’Brien says, is to be able to share the stage with other musicians whose work he loves. There are the folks in his outfit, sure — Roberts the guitarist, Erik Kertes on bass, Ben Alleman on keys, and Josh Adams on drums (Rob Jensen filled in on Friday for Adams, who is on tour with the Fruit Bats). But there are all the openers, too, like Malena Cadiz tonight — an Americana singer-songwriter with a lush voice — or Sam Evian, who opened for them at Pappy and Harriet’s out in Joshua Tree a few weeks ago. Each night, he asks those openers to join them for a song or two. “I want it to be a hootenanny,” O’Brien says. “I want it to be something where we roll along and other people jump in. Because I have no future in the music business, but I can be like a small part of it.”

The Vigodas’ Teragram Ballroom Set List“7 Nights to Rock” – Nick Lowe“No Action/Radio Radio” –  Elvis Costello“Baby Let’s Play House” – Elvis Presley“You Can Have the Crown” – Sturgill Simpson“Werewolves of London” – Warren Zevon “Jump into the Fire” – Harry Nilsson “Hello Mary Lou” – Ricky Nelson (with Malena Cadiz)“Twenty Flight Rock” – Eddie Cochran“Forty Days” – Ronnie Hawkins“I’m So Tired” – John Lennon“Victoria” – The Kinks (with Gaby Moreno)“Proud Mary” – Ike and Tina Turner (with Gaby Moreno) “Who Do You Love” – Bo Diddley “Not Fade Away” – Buddy Holly (partial song) “Polk Salad Annie” – Elvis Presley “Up on Cripple Creek” – The Band

#3376. This TP-Link Wi-Fi 7 Travel Router Is 27% Off for This Early Black Friday Deal

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

A novel solution for connecting to the internet on the go, the TP-Link Roam 7 travel router is now down to $87.99 from $119.99 in an early Black Friday deal—marking its lowest price to date, according to price trackers. This is not a full-size home router but, as the name suggests, a compact travel companion that measures roughly the size of a paperback book, with foldable antennas so it slips easily into a bag.

More about convenience than chasing top speeds, you can use the Roam 7 as a standard router, connect it to public wifi to create a private network, or share your phone's internet through USB tethering. It also supports Ethernet input and USB modems, along with range extender and wireless client modes. That flexibility is particularly useful when you’re juggling a laptop, phone, and maybe a tablet and would prefer not to sign each one into a shaky network separately. Setup is straightforward through the TP-Link Tether app: scan a QR code, choose your connection type, and you’re online in a few minutes.

Once it’s running, the hardware covers the basics, with a 2.5 Gbps port for a wired connection like a hotel’s Ethernet jack, a 1 Gbps port for a wired device, and a USB 3.0 port for a storage drive or phone tethering. And since it draws power over USB-C (5V/3A), a basic power bank can keep it going through a long layover or a camping trip. As handy as it is on the road, though, it’s not meant to replace a full-size home router—even with its 5 GHz band and Wi-Fi 7 support—which will generally offer better coverage and more consistent speeds. Real-world performance also depends heavily on your connection and setup. USB tethering, for example, can feel slower than using your phone directly. It also leaves out features like automatic band steering, so you may end up managing networks yourself. Still, if you travel often or need a portable network hub for multiple devices, you’ll find it holds up pretty well.

#3375. MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display review: A lot more than touch

Apple unveiled the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display last week, and it brings some of the biggest changes to the Mac in years. There’s a tandem OLED screen, a significantly lighter design, and the long-awaited addition of touch. Oh, and the Apple logo glows again.

Here’s what it’s like actually using the new MacBook Pro.

In 2016, Apple unveiled an all-new MacBook Pro design that prioritized thinness and portability above almost everything else, kickstarting what proved to be a rocky period for Apple laptops. The thinner, lighter MacBook Pro was marred by the butterfly keyboard, poor thermals, and an overall focus on form over function.

In 2021, Apple righted the ship. It unveiled a completely redesigned MacBook Pro that reversed many of those controversial decisions, bringing back ports, replacing the Touch Bar with a physical function row, and dramatically improving performance with Apple Silicon.

There was a trade-off, though: the MacBook Pro got bigger and noticeably heavier. The smaller model grew from 13 inches and 3.1 pounds to 14 inches and 3.5 pounds, while the 16-inch model went from 4.3 pounds to 4.7 pounds.

At the time, we were all willing to make that compromise. Now, with the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, Apple is once again making its pro laptops lighter — but without sacrificing what made the 2021 redesign so great.

The 14-inch model has dropped from 3.5 pounds to just 3.0 pounds, while the 16-inch model has gone from 4.7 pounds to 4.0 pounds. In fact, both new MacBook Pro models weigh essentially the same as their 2016 counterparts, despite having larger displays, significantly more powerful hardware, and none of the compromises that defined that generation.

Both models are also slightly thinner than before, with the 14-inch model measuring 0.59 inches thick (down from 0.61 inches) and the 16-inch measuring 0.63 inches (down from 0.66 inches).

How did Apple pull this off? The biggest change is the switch from mini-LED to OLED. Because OLED doesn’t require a separate backlight, Apple could make the display assembly significantly thinner and lighter. The company is also using custom on-cell touch technology to integrate touch sensing into the display panel, instead of adding multiple separate layers.

But while the new display technology played a major role, the weight reduction also came from countless other smaller engineering optimizations throughout the machine.

You notice the lighter weight of the new MacBook Pro immediately when you pick it up. My review unit is the 16-inch MacBook Pro, and I’m genuinely surprised at how nice it feels. It’s not light, but it feels less like a tank.

I’ve always used the smaller of the two MacBook Pro models for portability, most recently a 14-inch M4 Pro. The weight of the new 16-inch MacBook Pro has me reconsidering that preference, though. It feels remarkably nice for a laptop with such a large display, and I’ve really enjoyed having the extra screen space without feeling like I’m sacrificing too much portability.

The new MacBook Pro also features slimmer bezels around the display. Apple has eliminated the thicker bottom bezel, and for the first time, all four corners of the display are rounded. It’s a relatively small change, but I think it gives the MacBook Pro a cleaner, more symmetrical look.

And finally: the glowing Apple logo is back. Unlike older MacBooks, which used light from the display’s backlight to illuminate the logo, the new OLED MacBook Pro has no backlight to draw from, requiring a different approach.

The logo’s brightness is still tied to the display brightness, just like it was a decade ago. The higher your display brightness, the brighter the Apple logo on the back. It also factors in your environment’s ambient brightness.

When the MacBook Pro is closed, the logo looks like polished metal, just like it has since the 2016 redesign. Open it up, and it glows. It’s unnecessary, but I’m so thrilled it’s back.

The display is what Apple is most proud of on this new MacBook Pro. After all, the full marketing name is apparently “MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display.” It doesn’t exactly roll off the tongue, but I think it shows what Apple sees as the big differentiator compared to other MacBook Pro models it still sells.

And rightfully so. The PROLED XDR Display is stunning. It’s a major upgrade over the mini-LED display that Apple debuted in the MacBook Pro back in 2021 (which was no slouch, to be clear). The OLED panel’s color saturation, contrast, and deep blacks are miles better than any other laptop I’ve seen, including Windows PCs with high-end OLED displays.

The viewing angles are also noticeably better, with colors and brightness staying remarkably consistent even when you look at the display from the side.

One downside of the MacBook Pro with mini-LED is blooming. Because the mini-LED display used local dimming zones, there was a subtle halo around bright objects against dark backgrounds. With the OLED display on these new MacBook Pros, every pixel is independently illuminated, so that blooming effect is gone.

If you’re worried about burn-in, Apple says the new MacBook Pros have a revamped display engine that continuously monitors pixel usage, temperature, and other factors. It compensates individual pixels in real time to mitigate burn-in and maintain brightness. We’ll have to wait and see whether this holds true over time, but anecdotally I haven’t noticed any burn-in on my OLED iPad Pro after more than two years.

The improvements on the new MacBook Pro’s display go well beyond simply being OLED. Brightness is another area Apple emphasizes.

In direct sunlight by a window or on the patio, the display gets more than bright enough to remain easily readable. I rarely find myself needing to crank the brightness all the way up.

Those brightness improvements dovetail nicely with another area of emphasis on the new MacBook Pro: reflectivity. The new MacBook Pro’s glossy display has just 1% reflectance, which Apple says is due to two things. First, the OLED panel itself is designed to minimize reflections. It also has a custom antireflective coating that reduces reflections from the cover glass.

My review unit has a standard glossy display, and my previous MacBook Pro was a 14-inch model with nano-texture, so I’ve been paying especially close attention to the differences in reflectivity.

As I write this review, I’m sitting next to a large window that gets a lot of direct light. I’m very impressed with how well this glossy 16-inch MacBook Pro display handles reflections. It’s not, of course, as antireflective as my 14-inch MacBook Pro with nano-texture. But it’s much closer than I expected, and significantly better than my glossy MacBook Air.

I haven’t had a chance to try the nano-texture on the new MacBook Pro with PROLED, but Apple says the nano-texture is now “precisely etched into the cover glass,” so it should be even better than before.

All told, the PROLED XDR Display is impressive by every metric, both on paper and in the real world. Whether it’s the core improvements of an OLED panel, improved reflectivity, or higher brightness, you’ll notice the better display from the moment you turn the MacBook Pro on.

There’s something uncanny about using the new touchscreen MacBook Pro for the first time. This is still unmistakably macOS, with the same interface and software controls that we’ve known for years. Except now, you can reach out and touch the screen … and it actually responds.

Apple famously resisted adding touch to the Mac until now. Steve Jobs called the idea of a touchscreen Mac “ergonomically terrible” in 2010.

When Apple announced these touchscreen MacBooks, that clip of Jobs went viral. As usual, Jobs’ comments have more nuance than last week’s social media reaction suggests.

“Touch surfaces don’t want to be vertical,” Jobs said at the time. “It gives great demo, but after a short period of time you start to fatigue, and after an extended period of time, your arm wants to fall off.”

A lot has changed since those comments from Jobs, but I don’t think adding touch to the MacBook Pro proves him wrong. The ergonomics of using a touchscreen as the primary input method on a laptop-style device are, in fact, terrible. Your arm does get tired.

The good news, however, is that Apple is very intentionally not trying to make touch the primary interaction method on these new MacBook Pros. It’s clear from both using this touchscreen MacBook Pro and Apple’s own messaging that touch is intended to be a secondary input method. It’s there when you need it or want it, but you can also ignore it completely and never feel like you’re missing out.

So, with that out of the way: what’s it like using a touchscreen MacBook Pro?

Apple has made a variety of small tweaks throughout macOS to accommodate touch input. For example, when macOS detects touch input, items in contextual menus are spaced further apart.

When you long-press on something like an app icon in the Dock, it enlarges and shows you a more spaced-out list of contextual menu items. If you long-press an item in Finder, it lifts up under your finger, and you can drag it or drop it anywhere else.

The classic traffic light window controls also expand after you tap them. The first tap expands the controls without actually activating any of them. Then, tap a second time on the specific control you’re trying to activate. It’s a bit awkward having to tap the same spot twice in a row like that.

These tweaks are all about making macOS dynamically adapt to the fact that your finger is less precise than a pointer. Rather than redesigning macOS around touch, Apple has made the existing interface accommodate it when needed.

You also get all the typical touch gestures. You can pinch to zoom, swipe with four fingers to switch between Spaces or Mission Control, and swipe up to reveal the dock. You can pull to refresh in Safari, double-tap a window to fill the screen, and flick a window to the side to tile it.

Apple has also added automatic video stabilization that compensates for screen movement when you tap the display during a video call. This helps keep your camera feed steady, even when the screen itself wobbles slightly. It seems to work as advertised in my testing.

So far, I’ve found the touchscreen on MacBook Pro to be a “nice-to-have” addition, but not a reinvention of how I use the Mac. I catch myself idly reaching up to scroll a webpage instead of using the trackpad, tapping on the occasional Dock icon, and using pinch-to-zoom in the Photos app.

Touch input is also legitimately useful in places like iPhone Mirroring and the Xcode simulator. I can imagine people who regularly use rendering apps like Blender will find the touchscreen more useful than I do, since my primary job is manipulating text.

One reason I think touch might be less useful, or less important, on a Mac than on a Windows PC is that Apple’s trackpads are simply too good. There’s little reason for me to bother reaching up and using four fingers to swipe between Spaces when I can do it on the beautiful, big, glass trackpad. On a Windows PC with a crappy plastic trackpad? I bet multi-touch interaction is much more appealing on the touchscreen.

There have been a few instances where I just forget this MacBook Pro has a touchscreen until I reach up to flick a piece of lint or dog hair off the screen, and accidentally tap on something.

But I think that’s exactly how it should be. Using the touchscreen is a conscious choice, not a requirement. You can buy this computer and literally never touch the screen, or turn it off entirely via Accessibility in System Settings. For some Mac users, this is probably the most important thing. Apple hasn’t compromised the traditional macOS experience to accommodate touch.

The one thing that hasn’t changed with the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is performance. Much like the standard MacBook Pro models unveiled earlier this year, the new PROLED models are available with M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.

Apple says that the new MacBook Pro has a redesigned thermal system optimized for the new design, while also maintaining the same performance of M5 Pro and M5 Max we’ve come to expect.

My review unit is the 16-inch M5 Pro configuration with an 18-core CPU, 20-core GPU, and 48GB of unified memory. In GeekBench testing, the new MacBook Pro performs virtually the same as the models introduced earlier this year.

In my day-to-day use, I haven’t noticed any differences in performance or thermal behavior compared to my previous MacBook Pro. Admittedly, my workflow of writing, researching, editing photos, and dozens of Safari tabs doesn’t come close to pushing the M5 Pro to its limits. But the new MacBook Pro handles all of that effortlessly, without noticeable heat or fan noise. In fact, I haven’t heard the fans kick in once.

That’s not a definitive test of Apple’s claims about sustained performance, but it’s reassuring that the thinner and lighter design hasn’t introduced any noticeable compromises in my everyday use or in benchmarks.

This makes for an interesting predicament for MacBook Pro shoppers. Rumors say that Apple believes the M7 generation will offer such a dramatic improvement in performance, particularly around AI, that it’s skipping the higher-end M6 chips altogether.

The first M7 chips are expected sometime next year, likely late in the year for the high-end MacBook Pro. This means that if you buy an M5-equipped MacBook Pro right now, you’re buying a computer with a chip that will effectively be two generations behind in less than a year.

The M5 Pro and M5 Max chips are plenty fast, and these MacBook Pros also come with OLED, touch, and other changes mentioned throughout this review. Still, there’s something a little strange about Apple pairing its biggest MacBook Pro redesign in five years with chips that debuted eight months ago, particularly with the next major leap in Apple silicon reportedly on the horizon.

The Dynamic Island comes to the Mac for the first time with the new MacBook Pro. It never made sense to me that Apple added the notch to the MacBook Pro with so little software accommodation. The Dynamic Island finally addresses that, bringing a familiar iPhone experience to the Mac.

Live Activities now show up in the Dynamic Island, along with Now Playing info from apps like Music and Podcasts. For example, clicking (or tapping) the Dynamic Island while Music is playing brings up the mini player for easy access to controls. From the mini player, you can click again to open the full Music app. Live Activities from your iPhone also show up in the Dynamic Island on MacBook Pro, rather than in your menu bar like on other Macs. Spotlight on Mac bounces out of the Dynamic Island.

I’ve very much enjoyed having the Dynamic Island on the Mac. It’s one of my favorite iPhone features, especially for Live Activities. The implementation on the Mac is a great continuation of that experience.

Apple says that the new MacBook Pro has a redesigned six-speaker system that delivers 50% deeper bass. The speakers do indeed sound fantastic. Apple also specifically calls out improved speaker tuning when using the MacBook Pro with its lid closed and connected to an external display. In my testing, the difference is noticeable. The speakers sound less muffled and significantly louder.

Apple says battery life is unchanged on the new MacBook Pro models compared to the non-OLED variants.

I haven’t done any scientific battery testing, but anecdotally, my 16-inch M5 Pro model seems on track to match Apple’s claim of up to 17 hours of wireless web browsing.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is a fascinating product. It’s both a major evolution of the MacBook Pro and a better version of the same laptop we’ve come to love since its Apple Silicon reinvigoration in 2021.

The addition of touch is getting all the attention, but I think the lighter design is actually the more significant change in day-to-day use. I never expected a 16-inch MacBook Pro to have me reconsidering my longstanding preference for the 14-inch model.

Touch hasn’t fundamentally changed how I use the Mac, but it’s a welcome addition that feels overdue. People reasonably expect to touch their laptop screen and have it respond. Some people will undoubtedly find it more useful than I have, and Apple has done an excellent job integrating it into macOS without compromising the traditional experience.

With or without touch, the PROLED XDR display is a spectacular upgrade, with improvements in brightness, contrast, and reflectivity that you’ll notice every time you open the lid.

These new OLED MacBook Pro models command a $400 premium over the mini-LED M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pro models Apple is still selling. Those machines are also heavier, lack touchscreens, and miss some of the bells and whistles of the pricier models. Presumably, these two product lines will eventually converge, but right now the MacBook Pro lineup is a little awkward. The 14-inch PROLED model starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch starts at $3,399.

But that awkward positioning doesn’t take away from the product. This is still the same MacBook Pro we’ve come to love over the last five years. Apple has taken an already excellent laptop and made meaningful improvements to nearly every aspect of the experience. And it just so happens to have a touchscreen now, too.

#3373. Zohran Mamdani and Puerto Rican Band Chuwi Discuss Gentrification, Music, and Making Change

The Puerto Rican band Chuwi, made up of siblings Lorén, Willy, and Wester and their best friend Adrián, has spent the last couple years achieving international fame through a major collab with Bad Bunny, also ending up as his opening act on tour. But they’ve also used their platform to speak out about Puerto Rico — their debut album, Libertad, from last month, tackles government corruption, the economic and social effects of colonialist policies, and more — and on Friday, they joined Mayor Zohran Mamdani in San Juan for a conversation about issues central to the islands’ future.

As part of a visit engaging local organizations and community leaders, Mamdani sat down with the musicians to hear more about their perspective. “I look forward to listening to Puerto Ricans to hear about what the struggles are that they’re facing and how New York City can be a partner in fighting for working people wherever they may call home,” the mayor told Rolling Stone.

The meeting was part of the annual Somos Conference, where New York State lawmakers meet with Latino advocates over four days in Puerto Rico. The conference’s goal is to create a space where attendees can speak directly with those in positions of power about what’s most important to their communities.

This year marks the 40th anniversary of the event, and it is customary for the mayor of New York City to attend. Last year, Mamdani flew down just days after he was elected. This year, he returned, 10 months into his first term, and seemed clear-eyed about what he wanted to talk about during his 72 hours in town. His central focus is bridging the gap between the archipelago and the nearly 600,000 Puerto Ricans who call New York City home, with Mayor Mamdani targeting issues that matter to both.

“What I’ve heard from Puerto Rican New Yorkers is a concern about displacement and gentrification, not only in the neighborhoods that they’ve helped to build in New York City, but also right here in Puerto Rico,” he says.The mayor met with various coalitions and activist groups, such as Defend Cabo Rojo, FURIA, La Tejedora, and PR No Se Vende (“Puerto Rico Is Not for Sale”) that have dedicated themselves to combatting those challenges. But before those meetings, he scheduled an equally important sit-down with Chuwi, given their mission to spread the word about Puerto Rico’s struggles through their music. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Chuwi became a household name after they collaborated on the song “WELTiTA” off Bad Bunny’s Grammy-winning DeBÍ TiRAR MáS FOToS. They went on to be the opening act of his 59-date world tour. On Libertad, the band went back to their protest music roots and leaned more than ever into the politics. They’ve addressed some of these themes on the album since their earliest EPs, but never as directly as the LP.

Lorén initiated the conversation with Mamdani by describing how she was in New York City the week before the 2025 election. She told him she was impressed by the enthusiasm she saw for his campaign, saying that she found it very inspiring as a Puerto Rican. “What you guys are doing is inspiring,” Mamdani said, complimenting how they use their music to spread important messages without compromising the artistic side.

“When you’re not at a desk, it’s easier to tell the truth,” he said. He noted that as artists, they have the unique privilege of being able to speak out and that their music is a connection to home for many fans. Indeed, even Bad Bunny himself said last year that listening to Chuwi during his time living in Los Angeles pre-DtMF made him homesick.

Willy took the opportunity to ask Mayor Mamdani about how he’s been able to achieve so much in his term so far: “Why is it you can do these policies that other mayors couldn’t?” Related Content Puerto Rico’s Next Big Music Movement Is Pop Introducing Rolling Stone’s National Affairs Newsletter  Chuwi’s Debut Album ‘Libertad’ Is As Powerful As It Is Catchy Mayor Mamdani and Nas Have a Heart to Heart About Keeping NYC the Home of Hip Hop

“When you get elected you get disconnected,” Mamdani said. He explained that leaders can become cut off from the people they serve, and that the environment can turn into tinted SUVs and private hotel rooms. He gave examples of things he does “intentionally” to stay connected, like biking around the city. “Institutions change slower than people,” and too much patience sometimes inadvertently leads to complacency. “The more you stay with the people the more you stay impatient. You have to keep [them] around you,” he says.

Chuwi pointed out how skeptical many citizens are about politicians, and how cynicism has become the prevalent feeling, especially in a Puerto Rico that has been suffering economically for almost two decades, even before Hurricane María dealt a blow to its infrastructure in 2017.

Mamdani acknowledged that feeling, and said Puerto Ricans might be skeptical because “they know about history.” He said he’s aware of the gap between what politicians promise and what citizens actually expect them to deliver on. “How do you collapse that separation?” he said, sharing that he feels “inspiration” is a stronger force than “disillusionment” and that he tries to wake up every day “ready to fight” and to “use pressure in a productive way.”

Aware of how heated things can get in politics, and having been on the receiving end of a fair share of criticism, Willy asked how the mayor deals with mud-slinging and negative rhetoric in politics. Mamdani said that treating people who disagree with him harshly or with judgment leads to both sides feeling like there has to be a winner or loser in the debate. He stressed the importance of speaking to people who aren’t just “those who feel comfortable with you.”

Mamdani then pivoted to asking Chuwi about their future plans. The band said that they’ll be returning to cities they visited over the summer, hinting at a big tour of their own. Mamdani playfully reminded them he used to be an artist as well — as an indie rapper going by the alias Mr. Cardamom — and reminisced about how rough it was the first few years. “I was the opener to the opener to the opener,” he joked. “I once performed at 5 p.m. for a band that was playing at 9 p.m. I was singing to the seat savers.”He said he was delighted by the possibility of Chuwi going to different countries with their music, because as he put it, “through that, others will hear and see their own struggles.”

Lorén thanked the mayor for meeting with them, sharing that their grandparents were one of the families that moved to New York City during the post-WWII migration wave, and in fact got married in the city. Mamdani stressed the importance of Puerto Ricans in the history of New York, especially in organized labor movements. Lorén shared that her grandfather worked at a textile factory in the city.

Willy capped off the meeting by thanking Mayor Mamdani for meeting with the organizations working on the ground in P.R. He stressed how important their goals were when it came to pushing for the abolition of Puerto Rico’s tax haven status, protecting the coastal maritime-terrestrial zone, and trying to stop large developments that threaten Puerto Rico’s habitats like Esencia in Cabo Rojo and Moncayo in Fajardo, among other causes. “Politicians [in Puerto Rico] won’t meet with them unless it’s in a court room or public hearings,” he said. Trending Stories Good Riddance to the Cybertruck, the Chariot of the Dumbest Gods 'SNL' Cold Open: James Talarico Crashes Trump's Midterm Postmortem A Jesuit Priest Explains How He Facilitated Bob Dylan’s Meeting With the Pope 'SNL' Weekend Update Drags Trump Over Midterm Drubbing, Stephen Miller Promotion

Afterwards, Chuwi told Rolling Stone they felt inspired by the mayor’s words. “Being that he’s the mayor of New York, and New York has significant importance in Puerto Rico, it was super important to be able to discuss these matters with him,” says Wester.They also pushed back on critics who might accuse Mayor Mamdani of wading into issues outside his jurisdiction. “My counterargument is that we’re a colony of the United States, and New York is — and has always been — extremely important in Puerto Rico. We’re linked,” says Wester. “The rest of the world is watching what’s happening here on the island, yet our own politicians aren’t addressing it. I think it’s fair game.”

“It’s important to understand that this isn’t like the Financial Oversight Board. Just because people from outside — rather than locals — are addressing these issues, it doesn’t mean they’re coming here to exert control or anything like that,” Adrián says. “People hear ‘the United States is coming here to do things in Puerto Rico’ and immediately think, ‘Oh, Junta de Control Fiscal.’ No, it’s not [necessarily] that. It’s about creating a dialogue between the two sides.”As the meeting wrapped up and Chuwi said their goodbyes, the mayor snuck in one last question: are they doing a show in New York in the near future? Chuwi let Mayor Mamdani know they’ll be seeing each other again soon.

#3372. Instagram launches Edits for Mac with multi-track video editing and 4K exports

Instagram users can now download a Mac version of Edits, the company’s free video editing app, with multi-track editing, advanced color grading tools, direct publishing to Instagram, and 4K exports. Here are the details.

Instagram is launching Edits on desktop today, bringing its free video editing app to Mac with a larger workspace, more precise editing controls, and customizable keyboard shortcuts that can match those of other video editors.

Like Edits on mobile, Instagram says its desktop counterpart will receive weekly updates and is asking users for feedback to help shape future improvements.

A lot of creators have described the same moment to us: a project gets too big for your phone. You’ve got a dozen clips going, you’re trying to land a cut on the exact beat, and your thumb covers the part of the timeline you need to see. Your work is growing, and your tools should grow with it. We’re expanding Edits to take on your most ambitious projects on desktop.

One particularly interesting feature of the new desktop app is the ability to publish videos directly to Instagram, with support for native features such as tagging, location, and trial reels.

Instagram adds that it is expanding Edits to support “multiple aspect ratios (horizontal and vertical), with 4K watermark-free export, so you can easily share to any platform, or use Edits for personal projects.”

As for the actual editing tools, Edits for desktop makes basic operations like splitting, cutting, and trimming videos easier, while also offering a full multi-track timeline, keyframes for transitions, precise audio waveforms, and advanced color grading tools such as color wheels, curves, and log conversions.

Users can also import their own LUTs and fonts, customize keyboard shortcuts, and access Instagram’s licensed audio library.

Instagram says saved audio and text styles from the mobile app are already available on desktop. However, the ability to seamlessly edit the same project across Mac and mobile is still in development.

Instagram’s desktop Edits app also offers unlimited automatic captions with support for multiple languages, as well as hundreds of sound and video effects, all for free.

To download Instagram’s Edits for Mac, follow this link.

#3371. Meet the Rising Stars Competing for Best New Artist at the Latin Grammys

One of the most anticipated categories at the Latin Grammys is Best New Artist. In the past, the once-in-a-lifetime award has gone to people who have gone on to become major stars: Puerto Rican disruptors Calle 13, Colombian superstar Karol G, and Mexican singer-songwriter Silvana Estrada. Recent winners include Venezuelan prodigy Joaquina, Bogotá-based pop girl Ela Taubert, and Mexico City’s alt-star Paloma Morphy. For the 2026 ceremony, which takes place on Nov. 12 in Las Vegas, 11 upstarts from Latin America, the U.S., and Spain are hoping to take the honor next.

With 11 nominees this year instead of the usual 10, Rolling Stone caught up with four of the promising nominees ahead of the biggest night in Latin music. We spoke to Aria Vega, who is bringing the sound of Colombia’s Caribbean coast to the mainstream; rising Mexican-American singer Delilah, who has been blending genres with ease; Fabian, the son of Peruvian icon Gian Marco, who is blazing his own trail; and Mexican-Swedish maverick Sofia Monroy.

What does the nomination for Best New Artist mean to you?It means a lot because it represents more than just me. It represents my family, my people, my team, Barranquilla, and everybody who’s believed in me along the way. It also feels like an invitation to bring my world to a bigger audience. I’m still at the beginning of my journey, and having this kind of recognition gives me even more motivation to keep creating, experimenting, and showing people what I’m capable of. I’ve worked so hard to get here, and to have the music and everything we’ve been building recognized in this way is incredibly special. I’m grateful, excited and honestly just hungry for everything that’s still ahead.

How do you feel about representing Barranquilla and the culture of Colombia’s Caribbean coast?It’s a huge responsibility, but also something I do very naturally because it’s who I am. I don’t have to pretend to be from the coast or try to represent it in a certain way. It’s already in my accent, my humor, my music, my personality, and the way I see the world. I love showing people a different perspective of Barranquilla and the Caribbean coast. There’s so much creativity, beauty, character, and culture there. I want people to see us beyond the stereotypes and experience the coast through my eyes. If I can make somebody curious about where I’m from, or make someone from back home feel proud to see themselves reflected in what I do, that means everything to me. You recently met Shakira during her residency in Madrid. Meeting Shakira was incredibly special. She’s someone who has represented Colombia and Latin culture on a global level for so many years, so being able to share that moment with her was surreal. She’s opened doors for so many Colombian artists and I have so much respect for what she’s built. Of course I’d love to work with her one day! Imagine two Barranquilleras in the studio together. That would be something very special. I think we’d have a lot of fun!

What can we expect from your debut album that you’re working on?My album Costeñita Core is my baby. It’s a project where I’m putting together all the different pieces of who I am and the world I’ve been building. It’s very personal, but it’s also playful, colorful, feminine, a little chaotic, and full of personality. Musically, I want people to discover different sides of me. I’m exploring sounds, emotions, and ideas while staying connected to my Caribbean roots. Visually, I’m also putting a lot of myself into the project. I want people to feel like they’re stepping into my world when they listen to it. It’s my universe, my perspective, and my way of showing people what “Costeñita Core” really means. I’m so excited for everyone to finally experience it.

How do you feel about being nominated for Best New Artist?It’s honestly a dream come true. It’s one of those things you hope and dream about as an artist, but you never really know if or when it’s going to happen. To be recognized by my peers, fellow musicians, and members of the Latin Recording Academy is such a huge honor. It means that the music I’m putting out into the world is being heard, and that means everything to me. It’s also a reminder of how far I’ve come and all the people who have believed in me and supported me along the way. I know there is still so much I want to do and so much I want to explore as an artist. This nomination makes me even more excited to keep creating, growing, and sharing my music with the world. What does it mean for you to represent women in música mexicana in this category?It’s a huge honor and something I take very seriously. I want to do the category justice and make sure my voice and my sound are heard and heard well. I want to represent my music, my fans, and everyone who has supported me in a way that makes them proud. Música mexicana has such a rich history. I feel incredibly lucky to be part of a generation that gets to bring new ideas and sounds into the genre while still honoring its roots. I hope I can contribute something meaningful to that. This is especially meaningful to me as a young woman, but also as a big sister. I take that responsibility seriously because I know how important it is for young girls to see women being themselves, having a voice, and making their own choices. I hope I can show other young women that they don’t have to fit into a certain mold to belong in this industry. They can be themselves and do things their own way.

How would you say that being both Mexican and American influences the way that you make music?It influences my music in so many ways, sometimes in ways I don’t even think about consciously. Growing up in a bilingual household, both cultures have always been part of my everyday life. You can hear it in the way I mix English and Spanish, in different touches throughout my songs, and even in the way I express myself. My background, the music I grew up listening to, and the different influences around me are all incorporated into what I create. I don’t feel like I have to separate those parts of myself. They’re both who I am and I think that combination is a big part of my sound.

What was the experience like opening for Natanael Cano’s concerts at the Estadio GNP Seguros in Mexico City?It has been an incredible experience both times. Mexico City has such an amazing energy, and being able to perform there and share my music with those audiences, especially opening for an artist like Natanael Cano, is something I’ll always remember and those experiences hold a really special place in my heart. It’s also meaningful to be the only woman to have had that opportunity. I feel proud to represent women in that space and show that I can be myself and do things my own way. I don’t feel like I have to change who I am or fit into a certain expectation to belong on that stage. Being able to connect with those audiences while staying true to myself has made both experiences even more meaningful.

What does it mean for you to be nominated for Best New Artist?It still feels pretty surreal. I think it’ll really hit me once I get to Vegas. It’s something I’ve dreamt about for a long time, especially because it’s one of those things you only get to experience once in your career. I’m mostly excited about the opportunity to represent Peru and show people just how much talent and how many new, interesting proposals are coming out of our country. I feel really proud to be part of that.

Your sister Nicole was previously nominated for Best New Artist in 2022. How do you feel about following in your family’s legacy?My family was incredibly excited [about the nomination]. They’ve seen all the work and love that’s gone into this since day one. Nicole actually cried when I called her, which was really sweet. I can only imagine what it’s like to see your little brother experience something you’ve experienced yourself. I’m especially excited that my first Grammy experience is something I get to share with her, especially since she’s also nominated twice this year. It’ll definitely make the whole thing even more special. I’ve always thought that sharing music with my family is one of the biggest blessings. It’s pretty much all we’ve ever known at home. Growing up, I was always taught to approach this career with a lot of respect, love, and appreciation for what it means to make music. I think those values have stuck with me from the beginning. At the same time, I want to find my own way of doing things and build something that feels very much like me.

How are you carving out your own space in Latin pop music?When I moved from Lima to Los Angeles at nine, I was suddenly exposed to so many different kinds of music. I would go to festivals, discover new artists every week, and find myself getting really excited about all these new sounds and proposals. A lot of what I was hearing resonated with me, but when I tried to find something with a similar approach in Spanish, I couldn’t really find it. I think that’s where the idea for my project started. I wanted to bring some of those Anglo-inspired sounds into Spanish-language music, without losing the way I naturally write and express myself. I guess I’m trying to create the kind of music I wish I had more of when I was growing up.

What can we expect from you next?I’m currently wrapping up everything for my debut album, which is coming out next year. It’s been an insane process. I started writing the first demos back in July 2025, so the fact that I’m now finishing everything in November 2026 feels pretty crazy. I’ve always been an album person. I think there’s something really special about creating a complete project, and I hope we never lose that culture of making albums.

How do you feel about being nominated for Best New Artist?It means a lot, especially because it feels like recognition of a journey that hasn’t necessarily been linear. I’ve spent years figuring out who I am as an artist, experimenting, making mistakes, and finding my own voice. I think being nominated is a beautiful reminder that there’s space for different perspectives and ways of making music. But more than anything, I see it as a confirmation that you should always trust your intuition and follow your own path, even when it doesn’t necessarily make sense to anyone else at the time. Sometimes you just have to trust that little voice in your head.

Would you say that being both Mexican and Swedish influences the way that you make music? I think growing up between two cultures has shaped almost everything about the way I see the world, and naturally, that translates into my music. I’ve always felt like I exist somewhere in between, never entirely one thing or the other. But I’ve also come to realize that I don’t necessarily have to choose. I think I’m a walking contradiction in many ways. I’m made up of two cultures, two languages, two very different ways of seeing the world, and sometimes those things coexist beautifully, and sometimes they clash. I think that’s something that has become a big part of my artistic identity. I’ve stopped trying to make all those different parts of myself fit together into one coherent picture. They’re all equally me. You’re nominated for your Best New Artist for your album Morena. What do you want people to take away from that album?I want people to feel something. Morena was born out of a personal search, an attempt to make sense of a lot of things I was experiencing at the time: identity, belonging, grief, love, my roots, and my relationship with life and death. But I think one of the most beautiful things about making music is being able to connect with people through emotions. To share something so personal and have someone on the other side of the world recognize a piece of themselves in it. I think that’s quite extraordinary.

#3370. There's a New Way to Automatically Back Up Your Android Photos for Free

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you're an Android user looking for a way to save your photos and videos without maxing out your cloud storage space, your device may soon be able to back up automatically to your PC. As spotted by Android Authority, Google included automatic backups from Android to Windows via Quick Share in its release notes for Google Play services v26.43.

Quick Share is a wireless file-sharing feature for Android that allows users to send photos, videos, and documents to nearby devices, including Windows computers and iPhones with AirDrop. The new automatic backup feature, which is likely to roll out gradually, uses Quick Share's functionality to transfer copies of photos and videos on your phone to your PC when nearby.

Since these backups happen locally, you don't need to rely solely on cloud storage in your Google account, nor do you need to remember to initiate transfers of photos and videos between devices. Plus, this is all free and doesn't require a separate cloud service subscription. While you can back up your media to Google Photos, as of earlier this year, more data from your Android backups count toward your Google Account storage cap unless you exclude specific types. Alternatively, you can also cobble together a decent amount of cloud storage from other providers at no extra cost, but automatic backups between Android and Windows minimize the likelihood that you'll forget to save data, and your PC provides plenty of space for free.

Once the feature is available on your device, you'll be able to initiate backups in the Quick Share for Windows app. Your Android and Windows devices must be in close proximity and signed into the same Google Account. You can toggle Automatic backups on and change the settings for what gets backed up and to where. The transfers will then occur wirelessly in the background.

As Android Authority reports, early hints at this feature suggested that Samsung phones and PCs would be excluded from automatic backups, but the release notes don't specify any further details.

Emily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City.

#3369. WhatsApp adds shareable event invites and a new Events hub

WhatsApp is rolling out an update to Events just in time for holiday get-togethers. Guests can open an invite link, see the event details, and RSVP without creating a WhatsApp account or downloading the app.

When you create an event, you can add a cover photo and share the invite link by text or email. WhatsApp also gives you the option to share a QR code.

WhatsApp says your phone number is hidden from guests you don’t know, and “guests without a WhatsApp account will only see the event address after they RSVP.”

You could already create events in WhatsApp group chats and one-on-one conversations.

With this update, WhatsApp is adding a dedicated Events section in Settings where you can create invites, manage RSVPs, and see past and upcoming events you’ve organized or been invited to.

You can also set custom reminders and give guests the option to bring a plus-one.

WhatsApp says the updated Events feature will roll out to everyone over the next few weeks.

Apple Creator Studio updates were announced late last month, with what the company describes as “powerful new AI features” using a combination of Apple Intelligence and OpenAI models.

At the time, Apple didn’t give a specific availability date beyond sometime in November, but the updates are rolling out today …

Final Cut Pro for Mac now includes built-in MotionVFX — an expansive collection of visual effects, plug-ins, transitions, templates, and motion graphics tools — as well as seamless editing in Pixelmator Pro. Apple’s curated Content Hub now includes video assets and is available in Final Cut Pro.

Music creators using Logic Pro for Mac gain a new intelligent assistant in beta, an enhanced Stem Splitter that now separates drums, and a redesigned Browser that incorporates all sounds, with music understanding and even a Splice library.

Pixelmator Pro introduces Generate Fill, which lets creators transform selected areas of an image using natural language.

The headline news here is MotionVFX for Final Cut Pro.

Editors can also tap into the Content Hub directly within Final Cut Pro and access a library of Apple-curated stock videos, photos, and backgrounds to fill gaps, add polish, or spark new ideas without leaving their workflow.

Also notable is that the inclusion of OpenAI models alongside Apple Intelligence.

A new intelligent assistant powered by a combination of Apple-built models and OpenAI joins Logic Pro for Mac, helping creators and producers navigate production workflows, start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt, or refine an active project.

In Keynote, the intelligent assistant helps with designing, animating, and refining slides. In Pages, it drafts, restructures, and fine-tunes written content. In Numbers, it calculates, visualizes, and organizes data; recommends suitable chart types with a one-tap preview; and builds custom tables using world knowledge.

New MCP support, built on this platform, enables external AI agents and tools to read content, perform edits, and execute automated actions directly in Keynote, Pages, and Numbers.

If you have a DIY enthusiast on your list—or if you just want some new tools for your own projects—Black Friday sales are a good time to snag low prices on quality tools. Lots of big box stores are looking to thin out their inventory and make room for next year’s upgrades, so in addition to encouraging a holiday rush, retailers are motivated to price things to move. If you know what to look for, you can get up to 65% off on trusted brands. Here are a few of the best deals out there right now.

If you’re building a new cordless tool set, or updating your battery system, getting a cordless tool set can save you some money because these combos usually include batteries and a charger, which can be the most expensive part of your tool set. Here are a few of the best early Black Friday deals on cordless tool sets.

The Ryobi 6-tool 18-volt combo set is on sale for $199, 33% off its regular price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, a circular saw, a sawzall, an oscillating multi-tool, a work light, a 1.5-amp-hour battery, a 4-amp-hour battery, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted home tool brand.

The Ryobi 18-volt drill and driver set is on sale for $99, 34% off its usual price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, two 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a great starter set because it has the first two tools you need for a cordless kit and it comes with batteries so you can expand your set for cheaper as you develop your skills.

The Ryobi 4-tool, 4-volt project set is on sale for $99, 61% off its typical price at Home Depot. This set comes with a rotary tool, a project light, a glue pen, a mini drill, two rechargeable batteries, a charging cable, a set of starter rotary bits, and three glue sticks. This set is handy for DIY projects that require fine detail, like wood carving, craft projects, or framing pictures.

The DeWalt drill and driver combo set is on sale for $129, 46% off its regular price on Amazon. This set includes a drill, an impact driver, 2 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted brand for drills and drivers, and a good start for a cordless DIY tool set.

If you have a cordless tool set already and you want to expand your kit, or if you have a DIYer in your life who already has a particular brand of battery and you want to get them something they can use, a single tool deal can be just the thing.

The DeWalt 20-volt compact drill/driver is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 45% off its usual price. This tool comes with a 20-volt, 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. It’s a good first tool for a set.

The Milwaukee 18-volt impact wrench is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 68% off its typical price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. This is a good tool for driving bolts through tough materials and for automotive projects.

The DeWalt 20-volt oscillating multi-tool is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 50% off its regular price. This tool comes with a 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it's ready to use out of the box. This is one of the most versatile cordless tools, allowing you to cut a wide range of materials and use a sanding attachment to do finishing work as well.

The Milwaukee 18-volt tire inflator kit is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 65% off its usual price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to go right out of the box. This is an excellent addition to your emergency roadside tool set because you can use it to inflate a car tire with the charged 18-volt batteries.

The DeWalt 12-volt cordless powered ratchet is on sale at Lowe’s for $99, 50% off its typical price. This is a tool-only deal, so you’ll need a DeWalt 12-volt battery and charger to use it. This is a good tool for working on cars or for home appliance maintenance because it can fit into tight spaces.

The Makita 18-volt cordless electric 2-inch brad nailer is on sale on Amazon for $336.19, 36% off its regular price. This is a tool only deal, so you’ll need a Makita 18-volt battery and charger to use it. This is a good tool for attaching trim or paneling.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.
